title: Civilian Climate Corps Bill Returns to Congress - EarthTimes
description:
The Civilian Climate Corps proposal returned to Congress on September 24, 2026, when Senator Edward J. Markey and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez reintroduced the Civilian Climate Corps for Jobs and Justice Act.
What The Civilian Climate Corps Bill Would Do Civilian Climate Corps Benefits And Scope The proposal would create service positions connected to climate and community resilience.
The Civilian Climate Corps bill, as described in the research, seeks the broader statutory route.
Civilian Climate Corps Policy Stakes The renewed push for a Civilian Climate Corps reflects a larger question in federal climate policy: whether climate investment should be designed mainly as infrastructure spending, workforce development, community repair, or some combination of the three.
Until then, the Civilian Climate Corps for Jobs and Justice Act remains a significant climate policy proposal awaiting congressional action.
text:
The Civilian Climate Corps proposal returned to Congress on September 24, 2026, when Senator Edward J. Markey and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez reintroduced the Civilian Climate Corps for Jobs and Justice Act. The confirmed action was legislative reintroduction, not enactment. As of September 28, 2026, the measure remained a proposal, and the research provided does not identify a floor vote, committee vote, enacted appropriation, or signed law.

The bill sits at the intersection of climate policy, labor policy, public service, and environmental justice. Its stated aim is to create a large federal service program administered by AmeriCorps within the Corporation for National and Community Service. The reintroduced measure would focus on work tied to clean energy, climate resilience, environmental remediation, conservation, and sustainable infrastructure, according to the lawmakers’ September 24 announcement on the bill reintroduction.

The scale proposed is substantial: 1.5 million Americans over five years. That number signals a policy ambition beyond a demonstration program, but the legislation still faces the ordinary congressional hurdles of committee review, budget scoring, negotiations, and possible amendment. Until Congress acts, the bill describes a policy design rather than an operating federal program.

What The Civilian Climate Corps Bill Would Do

Civilian Climate Corps Benefits And Scope

The proposal would create service positions connected to climate and community resilience. The work areas described in the research include clean energy deployment, climate adaptation, environmental remediation, conservation, and sustainable infrastructure. Those categories are broad, and the final mix of projects would depend on implementation rules if the measure became law.

The bill also sets minimum worker protections and benefits. Corpsmembers would receive at least $15 per hour, full health coverage, and support services such as housing, child care, and transportation. The inclusion of those supports is significant because service programs can exclude lower-income participants if pay, housing, or caregiving costs make participation unrealistic. The proposed structure attempts to address that barrier directly.

Education benefits are another major part of the design. The research states that the proposal includes grants of $25,000 per year of service, with a maximum of $50,000, which could be used for further education or to pay down student debt. Those benefits would tie short-term service to longer-term career or education pathways. The bill’s backers describe those pathways as connected to good union jobs, though the exact labor-market outcomes would depend on future program rules, employer demand, and congressional funding.

Equity Rules In The Proposal

The proposal contains explicit environmental justice provisions. At least 50% of corpsmembers would come from environmental justice communities, and at least 50% of projects would take place in such communities. Tribal communities would receive 10% of dedicated environmental justice benefits. These provisions are central to the bill’s policy theory: climate investments should not only reduce emissions or repair environmental damage, but also direct employment and public investment toward communities that have been under-resourced.

The wording matters because a statutory target is different from a general preference. If enacted as drafted, agencies would need to translate those targets into eligibility standards, project selection rules, and reporting systems. The research does not provide those administrative details, so the degree of enforceability remains an unresolved implementation question.

How The 2026 Revival Fits Earlier Attempts

The 2023 Senate Bill And Its Status

The 2026 reintroduction followed earlier congressional efforts. In the 118th Congress, the Senate version, S. 2838, was introduced on September 19, 2023, and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, according to the official GovInfo record. The research states that the 2023 Senate measure did not advance to a vote. That history is relevant because it shows that support from bill sponsors did not translate into completed legislative action in that Congress.

A House companion bill was also introduced in the 118th Congress and expired at the end of that congressional session in December 2025 without enactment, based on the research provided. That means the 2026 action should be read as a renewed legislative effort rather than continuation of a bill already moving toward passage.

The earlier record also explains why advocates had looked outside Congress. In September 2023, legislators urged the Biden administration to create a climate service program through executive action while they continued to press for legislation. That executive route produced the American Climate Corps, described in the research as an initiative intended to train and deploy 20,000 service members for clean energy and climate resilience jobs. The American Climate Corps was modeled in part on the same concept, but at a far smaller scale than the statutory proposal.

Executive Action Versus Legislation

The difference between an executive initiative and a statute is central to the policy debate. Executive-branch programs can often begin faster when an administration has authority and funding mechanisms available, but they may be limited by existing appropriations and administrative priorities. A law enacted by Congress can define a program in more durable terms, set funding instructions, and impose eligibility rules. It also requires political agreement through the legislative process.

The Civilian Climate Corps bill, as described in the research, seeks the broader statutory route. That would give Congress a direct role in defining the program’s scale, benefits, equity targets, and administrative structure. It would also expose the plan to questions about cost, oversight, labor standards, and the division of responsibilities between AmeriCorps, other agencies, states, tribes, local governments, and community organizations.

The Policy Questions Still Unresolved

Scale, Cost And Administrative Capacity

The proposed scale of 1.5 million participants over five years raises practical questions. Recruiting, training, placing, supervising, paying, and supporting that many corpsmembers would require a large administrative system. The proposal assigns administration to AmeriCorps within the Corporation for National and Community Service, but the research does not provide a full operational plan for staffing, project approval, local coordination, or auditing.

Cost is another unresolved issue. The research notes that estimates for an earlier 2021 version of the concept were near $132 billion over five years, with projected per-corpsmember costs ranging from $40,000 to $70,000 depending on benefits, training, and education stipends. Those figures relate to earlier proposals and should not be treated as a final score for the 2026 bill. A current official budget estimate would be needed to assess the reintroduced legislation as written.

The benefits package is also central to cost and access. Pay, health coverage, housing, child care, transportation, and education grants would make service more accessible to people who could not afford a low-paid or unpaid program. Those same features would increase federal spending compared with a smaller service model. That tradeoff is a policy choice Congress would need to address through hearings, appropriations, or amendments.

Public Communication And Legislative Clarity

Public understanding of the proposal depends on clear distinctions between what exists now and what has only been proposed. The American Climate Corps was an executive-branch initiative described in the research as training and deploying 20,000 service members. The 2026 bill proposes a much larger statutory program. Confusing those two can lead readers to assume that Congress has already created the larger program, which the research does not support.

That distinction is especially relevant for climate policy reporting, where bill names, agency programs, and campaign promises can sound similar. Careful civic communication, including coverage from related public-affairs outlets such as policy communication coverage, can help separate enacted programs from pending proposals.

The confirmed status as of September 28, 2026, is narrow but clear: the measure was reintroduced on September 24, 2026. Its proposed benefits, workforce size, and equity targets are part of the legislative text or supporting materials described in the research. Its passage, funding level, administrative rules, and final program design remain unresolved.

Civilian Climate Corps Policy Stakes

The renewed push for a Civilian Climate Corps reflects a larger question in federal climate policy: whether climate investment should be designed mainly as infrastructure spending, workforce development, community repair, or some combination of the three. The bill’s structure points to the combination model. It would link climate-related work with paid service, education grants, support services, and targeted investment in environmental justice communities.

That approach has policy strengths and risks. A national service model could help connect young workers and career-changing adults with climate-related fields. It could also direct labor toward communities facing environmental burdens. Yet a large program would need credible oversight, clear project standards, measurable outcomes, and stable funding. Without those elements, a broad mandate could become hard to evaluate.

The legislative record also shows the limits of proposal-based policymaking. The 2023 Senate bill was introduced and referred to committee but did not receive a vote, according to the research. The 2026 reintroduction restarts the debate, but it does not settle it. The next meaningful indicators would be formal committee action, a public cost estimate, amendments, appropriations language, or a recorded vote. Until then, the Civilian Climate Corps for Jobs and Justice Act remains a significant climate policy proposal awaiting congressional action.

text:
An offshore wind turbine facility is to be created at the Port of Montrose, supporting about 80 jobs.

The factory, which will make components for off-shore wind turbines, is to be run by engineering firm Subsea Micropiles following a £5m investment.

A further £6.7m is being provided by the state-owned Scottish National Investment Bank, with Scottish Enterprise also pledging £1.45m.

First Minister John Swinney, during a visit to the site in Angus, said it would help ensure "benefits of the energy transition are retained in Scotland".

He also welcomed an announcement from SSE that the Port of Montrose is its preferred location for an operations base for the Berwick Bank B offshore wind farm, which is expected to create a further 100 jobs.

The Berwick project, set to be one of the largest offshore wind farms in the world, will see up to 307 turbines generating enough electricity to power up to six million homes.

Subsea Micropiles, which has offices in Ireland and Aberdeenshire, already has an operations base at the Port of Montrose.

The firm's new facility is expected to make parts for wind turbines in Scottish waters, and for international markets.

Chief executive Derek Robertson said: "Scotland has become an important base for our growth.

"We rely on the deep pool of talent, skills and offshore experience here to develop our technology, services and expand into a global market.

He added that the company's products "can be manufactured locally, with the potential to retain significant economic benefit in Scotland through engineering, vessel services and offshore supply chain".

Swinney said: "Scotland is already recognised as being at the forefront of floating offshore wind development.

"The investment behind today's announcements is a strong vote of confidence in the sector and in the skilled workforce, innovation and expertise that exists here.

"Subsea Micropiles' commitment to expand at the Port of Montrose will help ensure more of the economic benefits of the energy transition are retained in Scotland, creating high-quality jobs in Angus and the North East, supporting local businesses and strengthening our industrial capabilities."

text:
Greetings Agents of Impact!

In today’s Brief:

The power of place in Galveston, Texas

Perpetual funding for community development in southeast Alaska

Grocery stores in Boston transition to employee ownership

Expanding access to finance to expand access to housing

Featured: Power in Place

Power of place drives impact in a national movement of overlooked cities like Galveston. BOI energy, for “born on island,” is rebuilding Galveston, Texas, house by house, park by park and one small business at a time. Local leaders like Christine Bryant and Pastor Shirlyn Thomas have spent years stitching the storm-battered island back together, doing the unglamorous work of organizing residents, mentoring entrepreneurs, and building trust and investable projects that may just convince fleeing capital to stay in southeast Texas. Earlier this month, reinforcements arrived. The roving conference, Neighborhood Economics, and its national network of investors, church leaders and capital innovators, plus a freshly launched Texas Impact Capital Alliance, came to Galveston this month with a message: This has worked in our cities and it can work in yours. “We are designed to connect the wishes of Galvestonians to resources and make things happen,” said Bryant, who leads the local collaborative Vision Galveston.

Born on island. Vision Galveston formed in 2021 out of a nine-month community planning project that involved more than 8,500 residents developing a collective vision for the city’s future. The once prosperous island and birthplace of Juneteenth, where word finally reached Texas in 1865 that slavery had ended, has suffered decades of disinvestment and displacement, even as its culture and history remain intact. Build Galveston, Vision’s community development arm, has mobilized at least $2 million of a planned $5 million for The Galveston Essential Workforce Housing Fund. Incubate Galveston, powered by business builder Mortar, has graduated nearly 50 small business owners. A new Doers and Dreamers Fund will provide microloans to Galveston entrepreneurs that have completed Mortar’s business accelerator.

Fast, fearless and flexible. That energy isn’t unique to Galveston. Across the country, leaders in cities such as Cincinnati, Kansas City and Philadelphia are creating and sharing their own solutions. In Kansas City, LocalCode is tapping capital from charitable giving accounts known donor-advised funds, or DAFs, to deploy as low-interest loans and loan guarantees that leverage private capital to finance a pipeline of over $250 million in regenerative real estate from Black and Brown developers on the city’s east side. LocalCode’s Jeff Mendelsohn said DAFs represent “the biggest balance sheets in the country right now that can afford the type of return” required to unlock conventional capital for such deals.

Texas impact capital. As Galveston and other communities in Texas mobilize the supply of projects that deliver improved social and environmental outcomes, foundations, banks, healthcare institutions in the state are signaling increased demand for such investments. This summer, the Episcopal Health Foundation and Philips Foundation, working alongside the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, launched the Texas Impact Capital Alliance to bring more investment to projects that improve health and strengthen communities across Texas. Philips Foundation’s Kate Knight said the collaborative’s first investment vehicle will likely be “the least sexy investment opportunity you can imagine that is impactful in Texas.” Added David Erickson of the New York Fed, “Capital is not scarce, it’s scared. You can make your community, your neighborhood, investment ready. You can attract that capital if you’re organized.”

Keep reading, “Power of place drives impact in a national movement of overlooked cities like Galveston,” by Dennis Price.

Lessons for capital systems from a traveling greenhouse in southeast Alaska. “Moby, the mobile greenhouse, began traveling the Alaska Marine Highway in 2015 with a dream to set communities on the path to pursue new local food system solutions,” according to Kaylah Duncan of Spruce Root, a Native-founded nonprofit community development financial institution. The greenhouse carried plants, equipment and a curriculum from one community to another. The Yakutat Tlingit Tribe, for example, expanded a market-garden campus with a large greenhouse, hoop houses, berry production, composting, workforce development and traditional food knowledge. Situated at the end of a barge route, the Yakutat community knows how far food has to travel. “To shift the purpose of a system, you also have to shift who has the power to determine how resources flow, what takes priority, who matters and what is counted as a good outcome,” Duncan tells Spruce Root’s Alana Peterson and AlTi’s Brad Harrison in a post on ImpactAlpha.

Community capital. This week’s Agents of Impact Call (RSVP) will explore what capital can enable “by giving communities the resources, authority and time to build a future of their own making,” as Peterson and Harrison put it. To propel projects like Moby, it took an Indigenous-led coalition, the Sustainable Southeast Partnership, along with Spruce Root and an innovative perpetual fund. The Seacoast Trust’s perpetual fund provides the base layer of stability. “A community is not a portfolio of transactions,” the authors write, “but rather a living field of relationships, with memories of trust and distrust, reciprocity and extraction, and often both promise and disappointment.”

Perpetual funding. The Seacoast Trust, now with $32 million in assets, is a perpetual funding source for the Sustainable Southeast Partnership, which promotes the collective well-being and economic prosperity of Alaska Native tribes stewarding the coastal temperate rainforest. The Seacoast team, board and investment committee work with AlTi as investment advisor to balance financial resilience today with the ambition to create lasting impact over generations. The fund’s portfolio has expanded from global markets into decarbonization technologies, nature-based solutions and private investments, and plans to include place-based investments in Southeast Alaska. “As the people of Southeast Alaska say, ‘You cannot control the wind, but you can control your anchor,’” the authors write. The most durable return of all, they say: “Capital that not just performs but also holds a place, a people and a future together.”

Keep reading, “Lessons for capital systems from a traveling greenhouse in southeast Alaska,” by Spruce Root’s Alana Peterson and AlTi’s Brad Harrison.

Join The Call. Spruce Root’s Alana Peterson will explore this model of Indigenous-led investing with Sealaska’s former CEO Anthony Mallott, Ian Johnson of the Hoonah Indian Association, and AlTi’s Brad Harrison, and ImpactAlpha’s David Bank, Wednesday, Sept. 30, at 9am Alaska / 10am PT / 1pm ET. RSVP.

Dealflow: Ownership Economy

🛒 Family-owned grocer Tropical Foods goes employee-owned with Apis & Heritage financing. Roughly 100 workers have just become the new owners of Tropical Foods, a grocery retailer based in Boston’s Roxbury neighborhood that’s been owned by the same family for three generations. Apis & Heritage Capital Partners, investing out of its second employee-led buyout fund, provided financing to transition the company’s ownership to its workers, who serve more than 13,000 weekly customers in the greater Boston metropolitan area. “Tropical Foods is exactly the type of company we seek to partner with through our employee ownership strategy,” Todd Leverette of Apis & Heritage said in a statement. “The company has built an exceptional reputation over the past five decades by serving its community, creating jobs, and offering products that reflect the diversity of Greater Boston.”

Keep reading.

In other impact deal news:

🧑🏽‍🌾 Farm to table. New York-based Farm to People raised its first funding round since launching its fresh produce delivery service 13 years ago. The company secured $5 million in a round led by New Fare Partners, a women-led venture fund for food startups. Farm to People partners with small farms in the US and aggregates, boxes and delivers their produce for New York households. With the new funding, it will establish an aggregation facility in the Bronx next year. (The New York Times)

🏡 Retail impact. Cooperative investment company Kachuwa Impact Fund raised $4.2 million from new and existing members. The Colorado-based public benefit corporation manages an evergreen impact fund that invests in real estate and private companies (see, “Making co-ops work for investors, too”). It has more than 360 members, including 55 new members who joined the latest equity fundraising round. About 30% of members are non-accredited investors. (Kachuwa Impact Fund)

🌴 Catalytic capital. London-based Impact Earth launched a warehousing facility for nature-based projects in Latin America and Southeast Asia while it raises its Tropical Resilience Fund. The warehousing facility is supported by UNEP’s Restoration Seed Capital Facility and Porticus’ Good Energies Foundation. The Tropical Resilience Fund was incubated and supported by the Global Innovation Lab for Climate Finance, Convergence Blended Finance and the International Climate Finance Accelerator. (Impact Earth)

Impact Voices: Investing in America

Build more homes. Finance them better. America’s housing supply is short by about five million homes. “We need to build,” contributing Antony Bugg-Levine writes in his latest Investing in America column. The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law in July with overwhelming bipartisan support, cuts regulatory barriers, speeds permitting and encourages manufactured and modular housing. As the new housing law fuels supply, Bugg-Levine says, “investors, philanthropy and government need to make sure fair financing reaches the people and projects that can make that housing affordable and widely owned.” America has reinvented housing finance before, including in the 1930s with the development of the long-term, fixed-rate, amortizing loans that later became the standard 30-year mortgages, Bugg-Levine recounts. “How can we extend the benefits of our remarkable housing finance system and invent new financing for the people and projects it does not serve well?”

Fair share appreciation. Bugg-Levine’s book, “Investing in America,” highlights examples of financial innovation in housing, including Homium, which uses a shared appreciation mortgage to help buyers get into the housing market (Bugg-Levine serves as a senior advisor). In Colorado, Gary Community Ventures seeded the Colorado Housing Accelerator Initiative to finance housing for people who earn too much to qualify for subsidized housing but too little to afford high-end apartments. The new housing law seeks to lower the cost of manufactured housing; ROC USA helps residents organize cooperatives to buy the mobile home parks in which they own their homes. Writes Bugg-Levine, “Who gets financing helps determine who gets to own, who builds wealth, which developers can compete for properties, and how far scarce government subsidies can stretch.”

Keep reading, “Build more homes. Finance them better,” by Antony Bugg Levine. Catch up on all of his “Investing in America” columns here.

description:

text:
Please consider making a small donation to NYLCV as we work to set the stage for a successful legislative session and more in 2027. Clean here to donate.

As stakeholders convened in New York City for hundreds of events and conversations about energy, transportation, buildings, and more – Governor Hochul announced some big climate action.

Thank Governor Hochul for advancing critical funding and clean energy projects!

Here are the highlights:

The Governor announced a $1 billion investment in the Sustainable Future Fund (SFF) for programs that will save New York families money, reduce building emissions, boost agricultural resiliency, create green jobs, and improve air quality throughout the state.

$500 million dollars for building decarbonization and energy cost savings, including:

$150 Million for EmPower+

$150 million to assist eligible homes with affordable energy-efficient upgrades like heat pumps and weatherization, and more

$50 million for Clean Green Schools

$150 million for utility-scale thermal energy networks.

$200 million for the NY-Sun program and $100 million for NYPA Renewables in order to expand affordable renewable energy.

$25 million for municipal recycling and food waste

$25 million for climate resilient farming and $12.5 million for urban tree canopies

$25 million for land acquisition for state forests and parks, and repairs for public campgrounds, trails, pools, and recreational facilities

The Governor also announced a new Energy Infrastructure Development Plan to “update New York’s energy planning process with an actionable blueprint designed to cut through red tape and match resources with economic growth.”

IT TAKES LESS THAN A MINUTE:

TELL GOV. HOCHUL TO KEEP THE MOMENTUM GOING!

“For too long, our electricity and gas infrastructure planning have been done separately even though they have intersecting impacts,” said NYLCV President Julie Tighe in a statement following the announcement. “The Energy Infrastructure Development Plan will integrate the review of our energy needs and put us on the path to the lowest cost and cleanest options.”

All this and more is part of the Governor’s new Clean, Highly Affordable, Reliable, Grid Expansion (CHARGE) agenda, which is focused on driving down costs, holding energy companies and data centers accountable, building clean energy at scale, modernizing NY’s aging grid, and creating a clean energy economy

“The the $1 billion Sustainable Future Fund, along with a new cross sector energy planning initiative and advancing the new CHARGE initiative – and with projects ranging from climate resilient farms to zero-emission transportation – this investment is a welcome step towards a cleaner, more affordable future,” said Tighe

The Governor and NYSERDA also announced new large-scale renewable energy and energy storage infrastructure projects that total 1.7 gigawatts, including:

Eight contracted bulk energy storage projects – in New York City, Long Island, Hudson Valley, and Western New York – that will add 950 megawatts of new energy storage capacity.

13 awards for new land-based renewable energy projects — wind, hydroelectric and solar — totaling more than 719 MW of renewable capacity – enough to power over 230,000 New York homes annually.These projects will create more than 1,000 jobs and protect families from volatile fossil fuel prices and help keep our electric bills stable.

THIS IS EXACTLY WHAT WE NEED MORE OF: TELL GOV. HOCHUL TO KEEP IT UP!

“Governor Hochul is using Climate Week to deliver more clean power for New Yorkers,” said Tighe after NYSERDA’s announcement. “New York needs more electricity, and solar, wind, and battery storage are the fastest and most affordable ways to get it onto the grid. These projects protect families from volatile fossil fuel price swings and will help keep our electric bills stable.”

Additional funding:

$16.8 million is available through the Climate Resilient Farming Grant Program to help New York farmers reduce air pollution, protect water quality, protect and enhance soil health, and increase on-farm resiliency

$5 million for the development of New York’s clean energy workforce through the DEC’s Environmental Justice Green Jobs for Youth Grants that will support skills training by 20 community-based organizations helping advance green jobs for young New Yorkers

THANK GOVERNOR HOCHUL FOR ADVANCING OUR CLEAN ENERGY FUTURE!

These announcements are a major step toward New York’s clean energy future. Join us in thanking Governor Hochul for these investments and tell her to keep the momentum going!

Now is the time — help us seize the narrative from those seeking to stop our transition to affordable clean energy. They have spent untold dollars trying to sow doubt and instill fear into New Yorkers about rising energy costs, and to have us believe that the only way to keep our economy moving is to rely on fossil fuels.

We can’t let this moment pass. We need your help to ensure its the voices of countless New Yorkers who support homegrown clean energy that are heard – and not the small but loud opposition.

text:
All figures are in US dollars unless otherwise stated.

LEWISVILLE, Ark., Sept. 28, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Smackover Lithium, a partnership between Standard Lithium Ltd. (“Standard Lithium” or the “Company”) (NYSE.A: SLI) (TSXV: SLI), through its subsidiaries, and Equinor, through subsidiaries of Equinor ASA, today announced that it has amended its binding commercial offtake agreement (the “Agreement”) with Trafigura Trading LLC (“Trafigura”) for the South West Arkansas Project (“SWA Project” or the “Project”). The amendment provides the additional offtake volumes targeted to complete the Project’s customer offtake process and move to finalize the ongoing debt financing process.

Trafigura is a market leader in the global commodities industry, with an established presence across battery metal markets, including lithium. As one of the largest commodity traders in the world, Trafigura provides valuable access to multiple industry supply chains that rely on lithium chemicals along with a broad suite of customers.

Under the amended terms of the Agreement, Smackover Lithium now has the option, at its own election, to supply Trafigura with up to an additional 4,000 metric tonnes of battery-quality lithium carbonate in each year of the 10-year Agreement beginning at the start of commercial production. Combined with the initial 8,000 metric tonnes per year commitment under the Agreement, the maximum possible volumes to be delivered to Trafigura on a take-or-pay basis has increased to 12,000 metric tonnes of battery-quality lithium carbonate per year. Pricing and other key commercial terms remain subject to confidentiality.

The amended Agreement also provides valuable production flexibility for the Project. Because the additional volume is deliverable solely at Smackover Lithium’s election, it retains the ability to allocate that volume to other strategic customers in the future if a superior commercial or strategic opportunity emerges. Importantly, an additional offtake agreement is not required to move forward with the Project financing process.

The target for the SWA Project was to secure customer offtake agreements for roughly 80% (18,000) of the 22,500 tonnes of annual nameplate lithium carbonate capacity in its initial phase. Together with the recently announced binding take-or-pay agreement with LG Energy Solution for 8,000 metric tonnes per year, total possible commitments have now reached 20,000 metric tonnes of battery-quality lithium carbonate per year, exceeding the initial target.

Smackover Lithium now has sufficient offtake commitments to focus on finalizing its Project debt financing efforts. Due diligence and other customary processes in furtherance of Project financing are well underway with three major Export Credit Agencies. The Project continues to target a senior secured, limited recourse debt financing package of around $1.1 billion as outlined in its financing update on December 9, 2025.

David Park, Chief Executive Officer of Standard Lithium, stated, “This is a pivotal milestone for the SWA Project and a testament to the strength of our customer relationships. The offtake process has been one of the most important and time-intensive workstreams and we now have the volume commitments needed to support our Project debt financing, as well as the flexibility to continue to pursue transactions that maximize value for our stakeholders. Our path forward is clear as we focus on finalizing and closing the Project financing, taking FID and beginning construction.”

Having successfully completed the commercial offtake workstream, Smackover Lithium continues to target a Final Investment Decision (FID) on the SWA Project later this year before moving promptly into construction. This would enable first commercial production of battery-quality lithium carbonate in 2029.

Qualified Person

All scientific and technical disclosure in this news release was reviewed and approved by Mr. Stephen Ross, P.Geo., British Columbia, Vice President of Resource Development for Standard Lithium and a Qualified Person for purposes of, and as that term is defined in, National Instrument 43-101 – Standards of Disclosure for Mineral Projects. Mr. Ross is not independent of the Company.

Department of Energy Acknowledgement and Disclaimer

This material is based upon work supported by the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation under award Number DE-MS0000099. The views expressed herein do not necessarily represent the views of the U.S. Department of Energy or the United States Government.

About Smackover Lithium

Smackover Lithium is a partnership between Standard Lithium and Equinor, through subsidiaries of Equinor ASA. Formed in May 2024, Smackover Lithium is developing multiple direct lithium extraction (“DLE”) projects in Southwest Arkansas and East Texas. Standard Lithium is the majority partner with a 55% interest and is the developer and operator of the projects. Equinor holds the remaining 45% interest in the projects.

About Standard Lithium Ltd.

Standard Lithium is a leading near-commercial lithium development company focused on the sustainable development of a portfolio of large, high-grade lithium-brine properties in the United States. The Company prioritizes industry leading projects characterized by large high-grade resources, robust infrastructure, skilled labor, and streamlined permitting. Standard Lithium aims to achieve sustainable, commercial-scale lithium production via the application of a scalable and fully integrated DLE and purification process. The Company’s flagship projects are in the Smackover Formation, an attractive lithium brine asset, focused in Arkansas and Texas. Standard Lithium is advancing the SWA Project, a greenfield project located in southern Arkansas, and a promising lithium brine resource position in East Texas, including the highest known lithium brine grade project in North America, the Franklin project.

Standard Lithium trades on both the TSX Venture Exchange (“TSXV”) and the NYSE American under the symbol “SLI”. Visit the Company’s website at www.standardlithium.com for more information.

About Equinor

Equinor is an international energy company committed to long-term value creation in a low-carbon future. title: America's air monitors are disappearing. So is your power to expose polluters.
authors: Ames Alexander, Floodlight, Brad Racino, Floodlight, Ames Alexander, Brad Racino, Caity Coyne

text:
This story is from Floodlight, a nonprofit newsroom that investigates the powers stalling climate action. Sign up for Floodlight’s newsletter here.

Across much of the U.S., people have little way to know when the air they breathe turns dangerous.

Over recent decades, federal funding for public air monitoring has declined, the number of monitors has fallen, and much of the remaining equipment is aging or located far from major polluters.

Now, the stakes are rising: Wildfire smoke is reaching more communities, data centers are adding pollution, and climate-driven heat waves are worsening ozone levels. The Trump administration, meanwhile, has delayed and rolled back requirements meant to hold companies accountable for their emissions.

As the public monitoring system has weakened, communities have increasingly turned to an alternative: low-cost sensors they can use themselves.

But a Floodlight investigation finds industry is moving to restrict that option, too.

Since 2024, lawmakers in Louisiana, Ohio and Kentucky have passed strikingly similar bills — backed by chemical or manufacturing trade groups — that curb the use of community-collected data in enforcement actions.

The bills share a common thread: They block regulators from using air-quality data for enforcement purposes unless it meets EPA-approved standards. Similar bills in West Virginia have yet to pass.

In case after case, proponents have made the same argument: Community monitoring isn’t reliable enough for regulatory enforcement.

Yet when lawmakers in West Virginia offered a version of a bill designed to ensure accuracy, industry resisted.

The bill “essentially codifies what we are trying to prevent,” an official at the chemical giant Chemours wrote in an internal email.

An early-warning system in decline

Thousands of small, often-unremarkable instruments serve as the nation’s early-warning system for dangerous air — detecting pollution that people can’t always see or smell.

Some sit inside shelters the size of garden sheds. Others are mounted on rooftops or tucked into fenced compounds. Together, these monitors measure pollutants ranging from ozone and carbon monoxide to carcinogens such as benzene and vinyl chloride.

The network grew out of the 1963 Clean Air Act and transformed the way the nation tracked air pollution, giving regulators data they could use to identify dangerous conditions and hold polluters accountable. Since then, air pollution has fallen dramatically across much of the U.S.

But today, the network is “showing its age,” said Chet Wayland, who led EPA’s Air Quality Assessment Division for nearly two decades. “And it’s getting smaller over time.”

For example:

Leaks, termites and ants plague monitoring stations in one state while officials in another have resorted to shopping on eBay for discontinued parts, according to a 2020 congressional watchdog report.

Adjusted for inflation, federal grants to support the network have fallen more than 35% over the past two decades, while the Trump administration tried unsuccessfully last year to eliminate them entirely — and is trying again this year.

The number of government air monitors nationwide fell by nearly half over the same 20-year period, according to EPA data.

The decline was especially pronounced among air monitors that track toxic chemicals, including those linked to cancer and other serious health effects.

For example, the network monitoring vinyl chloride — the carcinogen at the center of the 2023 train derailment in East Palestine, Ohio — shrank by more than half from 2004 to 2025. So did the network for chloroprene and benzene.

Floodlight analyzed the largest industrial sources of air pollution in Kentucky, Louisiana, Ohio and West Virginia — where the monitoring legislation was introduced — and compared what each one reported releasing against what public monitors in those states are capable of detecting.

For 71 of the 100 facilities examined, the chemical they release most isn’t measured by any government monitor in the state.

Hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid, methanol — no air monitor currently reporting to the EPA measures those toxic chemicals.

Nelson Roque, an assistant professor at Penn State, co-authored a 2025 study that found nearly six in 10 U.S. counties have no public air monitor at all.

Such gaps matter most in communities already facing higher risks. Black and low-income people bear a disproportionate share of elevated cancer risks from air toxics, according to the EPA.

“We’ve realized the value of other infrastructure, and yet not this one,” Roque said. “Last I checked, we all breathe air.”

The shrinking public network has set the stage for another fight: Who gets to measure the air, and whose data counts.

Louisiana: A monitoring gap, and the fight to keep it

Public air monitors in Louisiana — a national hub for oil, gas and petrochemicals — are often located miles from major industrial polluters and fail to test for some of the most dangerous chemicals, a recent Floodlight investigation found.

Community groups have tried to fill that gap. A $500,000 grant awarded under the Biden administration’s Inflation Reduction Act would have allowed the Louisiana Environmental Action Network to establish air monitoring in 27 communities it identified as pollution hot spots.

But the group was able to install monitors in only four communities before the Trump administration canceled the grant last year.

“It’s like having your legs knocked out from under you,” said LEAN executive director Marylee Orr.

In 2024, meanwhile, Louisiana became the first state to restrict the use of community air monitoring data.

The Louisiana Chemistry Association helped draft the Community Air Monitoring Reliability Act (CAMRA), which cites the need for “science-based standards” and bars the use of air pollution data in enforcement or regulatory actions unless it’s captured by EPA-approved monitors. That equipment typically costs tens of thousands of dollars.

In a previous statement to Floodlight, LCA president David Cresson defended the law, saying it ensures “data used to enforce our state’s environmental protection laws complies with minimum U.S. EPA standards” and doesn’t stop residents from monitoring air quality for their own information — only from using unregulated methods for enforcement purposes.

The same period brought other rollbacks, some sought by the chemical industry’s most powerful national lobbying group. The American Chemistry Council — the LCA’s national counterpart — spent more than $22 million lobbying in 2024, ranking 10th among 9,200 organizations tracked by an independent watchdog group.

The ACC and the American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers last year requested a blanket two-year exemption from Biden-era regulations meant to cut certain toxic emissions by nearly 80 percent at roughly 200 chemical manufacturing plants. They didn’t get the blanket exemption — but individual plants that applied did.

So far, President Donald Trump’s EPA has granted more than 60 petrochemical facilities exemptions from the rule, and the agency is now weighing whether to rescind it entirely.

The ACC also successfully lobbied against federal rules that would have required about two dozen chemical plants to conduct fenceline monitoring for ethylene oxide, a carcinogen that contributes substantially to the elevated cancer risk in Louisiana’s Cancer Alley.

The national trade group did not respond to Floodlight’s questions about its lobbying or its involvement in Louisiana’s CAMRA law. Nor did it explain its role in promoting similar legislation in other states.

But in an emailed statement, the ACC said it has invested in community air-monitoring projects and “publicly advocated for expanded access to credible air quality information.” It said it supports monitoring that produces reliable, transparent data and gives communities and regulators information they can use to make informed decisions.

Kentucky takes a page from Louisiana

Odors from Rubbertown, an industrial complex that housed tire and synthetic rubber plants during World War II, have long bothered residents in west Louisville, Ky. So, in the early 2000s, the city’s Air Pollution Control District, the EPA and others launched a study that confirmed what residents had long known: The air had unacceptably high levels of toxic pollutants.

A plan was enacted, regulations were revised, and the air was continuously tested. More than 15 years later, regulators announced toxic air contaminants in the Louisville metro area were down by almost 80 percent — with the most dangerous chemicals cut by 96 percent.

Despite the success of expanded air monitoring in Louisville, Kentucky lawmakers have moved in the opposite direction. In March 2025, 10 months after Louisiana’s CAMRA law, they passed House Bill 137, which also restricted how air-monitoring data can be used in enforcement actions.

Lloyd “Rusty” Cress, executive director of the Kentucky Chemical Council, told the Kentucky Lantern that the bill was similar to Louisiana’s community air monitoring legislation. The law says air needs to be tested with “scientifically defensible” methods — echoing a phrase used in an ACC blog post in 2023.

The ACC, the American Petroleum Institute, Dow Chemical and Chemours all lobbied for it.

Jess Loizeaux, a Chemours spokesperson, said the company doesn’t object to community air monitoring. “We object to community air monitoring results being used for enforcement decisions without first verifying the validity and accuracy of the data through official tests performed by trained technicians at the appropriate regulatory authority,” she told Floodlight.

Kentucky’s political push unfolded against a backdrop of major gaps in public air monitoring. Only one of the state’s 25 largest air polluters is close to an air monitoring station that measures the top toxic chemical it emits.

Fewer than a quarter of the state’s counties have an air monitoring station.

Ohio’s restrictions meet with legal challenge

Ohio’s new air monitoring rule was tucked into last year’s budget bill with no named sponsor. It, too, stops regulators from acting on air-monitoring data collected by community groups.

“When we take away the ability for those folks to have a reasonably priced monitor … for their own protection, we’ve just taken any tool they had right out of their hands,” said Miranda Leppla, an attorney who sued the state over the new rules last year on behalf of environmental groups.

The lawsuit also challenges another provision in the budget bill that instructs state regulators to remove Ohio’s “air nuisance rule,” which allowed citizens to take legal action against companies whose emissions endanger public health.

One of the plaintiffs, Donna Ballinger, lives in Middletown, Ohio, hundreds of feet from a steel manufacturing plant that frequently rains down black, white and gray particles onto her house and yard, she said. Fumes sometimes burn her eyes and throat, she said, and she often holds her nose when walking between her house and car.

“My fear is cancer,” Ballinger told Floodlight.

She has an air monitor mounted in her front yard. But Ohio’s new requirement has made it impossible to use the data such monitors collect “as evidence of the nuisance conditions,” the lawsuit says.

The Ohio Chemistry Technology Council backed the measure. The group did not respond to Floodlight’s requests for an interview.

Tony Long, general counsel for the Ohio Chamber of Commerce, said businesses are concerned that uncalibrated air monitors will spread misinformation.

“Given our litigious nature in this state, we think that the guardrails make sense,” he told Floodlight. “You don’t want to be stopped for speeding on an uncalibrated speed gun.”

With more than 90 public air monitoring stations, Ohio has a more robust air monitoring network than some states. Yet none of Ohio’s 25 largest air polluters are within 20 miles of a public air monitoring station that measures its top toxic emission. In fact, no air monitor in the U.S. measures the chemical that 10 of them release most.

Ohio’s Syensqo Specialty Polymers plant, which makes a resin used in plastics, released more than 130 tons of volatile organic compounds into the air last year, according to Ohio regulators.

The nearest air monitoring station is about four miles away — in West Virginia — and doesn’t measure VOCs.

Industry resistance stalls West Virginia efforts

West Virginia’s Department of Environmental Protection runs just 14 monitoring sites in 12 counties. The other 43 counties have no state monitoring stations at all.

None of West Virginia’s 25 largest air polluters has a public air monitor within 25 miles that measures the pollutant it releases most. For 17 of the facilities, no air monitor anywhere in the U.S. measures their top toxic emission.

In 2024, a state bill backed by the West Virginia Manufacturers Association would have barred community air monitoring data from use in regulation, enforcement and lawsuits; it passed the House but died in the Senate — partly because industry couldn’t agree on what to include.

A compromise version of the 2024 bill, drafted to address the concerns of some lawmakers, would have let regulators use community data if the monitors met manufacturer standards. Industry refused to support it.

In emailed comments about the compromise bill, West Virginia Manufacturers Association Bill Bissett said it “neuters” the measure and was “now toothless.” Chemours’ Jeff Fritz wrote, “I do not like this draft,” and said the bill “essentially codifies what we are trying to prevent,” according to emails obtained by Mountain State Spotlight. Neither Bissett nor Fritz responded to requests for comment.

Subsequent bills, introduced in 2025 and 2026, also failed.

Why monitoring matters

Evidence shows that better monitoring can reduce pollution — and potentially save lives.

In 2018, the EPA made refineries begin monitoring benzene along their fencelines, and within five years, the number of refineries above EPA’s benzene action level dropped by half, according to a report by the Environmental Integrity Project.

While some states have made it difficult to know what’s in the air, others have been proactive:

California is funding equipment and training for residents in fenceline communities to monitor for things like pesticides, hexavalent chromium and other toxic chemicals. From 2017 to 2025, the state budgeted $1.4 billion to help communities that have historically been overburdened with air pollution.

Colorado required four industrial plants to install fenceline monitors that measure hydrogen sulfide, benzene and hydrogen cyanide in real time. The state also bought two mobile vans that regularly sample the same pollutants in surrounding neighborhoods.

The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality and its contractors operate 33 automated gas chromatographs — sophisticated equipment that collects air samples every hour and provides near real-time readings of volatile organic compounds.

But in much of the U.S, those who live near industrial plants still have little way to know what they’re breathing.

An unanswered question

Reonda Victor lives in Louisiana’s heavily industrialized corridor between Baton Rouge and New Orleans, where flares from industrial plants often illuminate the night sky.

Her mother, grandmother and sister all had breast cancer. Concerned about her own risk, she underwent genetic testing, which showed no predisposition to the disease, she said.

The closest public air monitoring station to her home — which lies in an area where air pollution poses one of the highest cancer risks in the country — tests only for lead.

Did industrial pollution cause the illnesses that struck her family members? She can’t say. But proper air monitoring could help answer that question, she said.

“Without information, we don’t know.”

text:
First Minister John Swinney has welcomed investment of more than £5 million by Subsea Micropiles to establish a new manufacturing facility at the Port of Montrose.

The new facility will manufacture components used to secure floating offshore wind turbines in deep waters in Scotland, as well as international markets.

The project is expected to create around 80 new jobs. It is being supported by £1.45 million funding from Scottish Enterprise, following a £6.7 million commercial investment delivered through the Scottish National Investment Bank, as part of the Scottish Government’s £500 million commitment to support offshore wind ports and supply chain.

During a visit to the Port, the First Minister also welcomed SSE’s announcement that the Port is its preferred location for the operation and maintenance base for its planned Berwick Bank B offshore wind farm, which is expected to create a further 100 new jobs.

First Minister John Swinney said:

“Scotland is already recognised as being at the forefront of floating offshore wind development. The investment behind today’s announcements is a strong vote of confidence in the sector and in the skilled workforce, innovation and expertise that exists here.

“Subsea Micropiles’ commitment to expand at the Port of Montrose will help ensure more of the economic benefits of the energy transition are retained in Scotland, creating high-quality jobs in Angus and the North East, supporting local businesses and strengthening our industrial capabilities.

“SSE’s selection of the Port as its preferred location for its operations and maintenance base for Berwick Bank further strengthens Scotland’s offshore wind supply chain and will create more jobs as well as investment in skills, infrastructure and local communities.

“Scotland’s ports are critical enablers of our offshore wind ambitions and key economic assets for surrounding communities, with the Port of Montrose set to become one of the world's largest offshore wind operations and maintenance hubs, supporting the Berwick Bank, Seagreen and Inch Cape offshore wind farms.

“Through our strategic investment in offshore wind, we are helping to develop the infrastructure, skills and supply chains needed to secure long-term economic growth and export opportunities from the global market.”

Derek Robertson, CEO at Subsea Micropiles said:

“Scotland has become an important base for our growth. We rely on the deep pool of talent, skills and offshore experience here to develop our technology, services and expand into a global market.

"Ultimately, we see significant potential to establish high-volume production of our anchor and foundation systems in Montrose as the market develops. These are scalable solutions which can be manufactured locally, with the potential to retain significant economic benefit in Scotland through engineering, vessel services and offshore supply chain.

"This funding support from Scottish Enterprise is an important part of enabling that next phase of growth and helping us establish the capability required to respond to future market demand.”

Stuart Hood, Director of Offshore Wind Operations at SSE Renewables, said:

“Scotland has built a world-class offshore wind industry, and today's announcement shows the economic opportunities that can follow when that expertise is matched with long-term investment.

“Our decision to choose Montrose as the preferred operations base for Berwick Bank B and create 100 new jobs reflects the strength of the port, its people and the local supply chain. SSE has built a strong relationship with Montrose Port over many years, and this latest long-term investment will help support the port's continued development as a leading offshore wind hub. This is clear evidence of the potential for the clean energy transition to drive skilled job creation and economic opportunity for communities up and down the country.”

Reuben Aitken, Managing Director Investment and International at Scottish Enterprise, said:

"Scotland has a world-class offshore wind opportunity, and innovative companies like Subsea Micropiles will be central to turning that opportunity into jobs, investment and long-term economic value.

“We're proud to support the company's expansion in Scotland through our £1.45 million funding, helping unlock more than £5 million of investment and create 81 jobs. By backing innovative businesses to establish and grow their operations here, we're strengthening Scotland's offshore wind supply chain, attracting high-value investment and supporting the technologies that will help drive the energy transition."

Background

Subsea Micropiles is full-service foundations company with offices in Westhill (Aberdeenshire) and a base of operations at the Port of Montrose. The project is being supported by a £1.45 million Regional Selective Assistance grant from Scottish Enterprise, following a £6.7 million investment delivered through the Scottish National Investment Bank: Subsea Micropiles | Scottish National Investment Bank

The Berwick Bank Wind Farm project represents one of the most significant renewable energy developments proposed for the UK. If built to its full 4.1GW potential capacity across all three phases, Berwick Bank could become the world's largest offshore wind farm on completion. At full production it would be capable of generating enough clean electricity to power more than six million UK homes annually through reliable, home-grown renewable power, making it a nationally significant project for the UK's long-term energy security and clean power ambitions.

text:
Another Chinese automaker has figured out how to charge an EV battery in around the time it takes to read this newsletter.

What happened: China’s Geely Auto unveiled an EV battery that can be charged from 10% to 70% in four minutes and 30 seconds. Geely said its technology incorporates AI to predict the temperature of a charging battery and adjust power flows accordingly.

BYD, another Chinese automaker, and CATL, a battery manufacturer, have developed their own “ultrafast” charging technology that also takes around five minutes.

Why it matters: The battery is the most expensive — and, arguably, the most important — part of an electric vehicle. Geely is one of several Chinese automakers bringing battery development in-house to try and bring down costs and reduce dependence on third-party battery makers, like CATL.

Faster-charging batteries also give Chinese EVs another advantage over competitors in Europe and North America, where the fastest chargers still typically take 20 to 40 minutes to bring a battery from 10% to 80% charged.

Zoom out: The breakthroughs in China’s battery industry contrast with the struggles of Canada’s nascent battery sector, which has been plagued by recent setbacks. Just last week, VW’s PowerCo announced it would delay the opening of its St. Thomas battery manufacturing plant until 2029. Earlier this year, Honda scrapped its plans to develop an EV supply chain, including battery plants in Ontario, and last year saw the collapse of the ambitious Northvolt battery project in Quebec.—TS

title: Trump administration set to roll out lower fuel economy standards for cars, light trucks
description:
NEW YORK (AP) — The Trump administration on Monday plans to release new fuel economy standards that would relax regulatory requirements for automakers to control pollution from gasoline-powered cars and light trucks.
Fuel economy requirements set out how far new vehicles need to travel on a gallon of gasoline.
The administration and automakers have said the new rules will increase Americans’ access to the full range of gasoline vehicles they need and can afford.
Without these standards, in 2035, cars could produce 22,111 more tons of carbon dioxide per year than under the Biden-era rules.

text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The Trump administration on Monday plans to release new fuel economy standards that would relax regulatory requirements for automakers to control pollution from gasoline-powered cars and light trucks.

President Donald Trump said on his Truth Social media account Saturday that the less stringent mileage requirements would “take the waste out of building cars in America” and save families “thousands on a new, beautiful and safe car,” while boosting auto production in the U.S.

Last December, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration projected that the new standards would set the industry fleetwide average for light-duty vehicles at roughly 34.5 miles per gallon in the 2031 model year, down from a projected 50.4 miles per gallon in 2031 under rules put in place by the Biden administration.

Fuel economy requirements set out how far new vehicles need to travel on a gallon of gasoline. The change would further make do on Trump’s promise to revoke policies that encouraged or created incentives for the production of electric vehicles.

Since taking office, Trump has relaxed auto tailpipe emissions rules, repealed fines for automakers that do not meet federal mileage standards and terminated consumer credits of up to $7,500 for EV purchases.

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said Saturday on his social media account on X that the changes would be announced Monday. The White House, Department of Transportation and NHTSA couldn’t immediately be reached for comment on the details of the new standards.

General Motors, Stellantis, and Ford Motor, maker of the top-selling pickup truck, the F-150, also couldn’t be immediately reached for comment. The administration and automakers have said the new rules will increase Americans’ access to the full range of gasoline vehicles they need and can afford.

The average new car in America sold for $50,089 in August, crossing over the $50,000 line for the first time since last December, according to Kelley Blue Book data. At the same time, Americans are spending more on gas as Washington’s war with Iran disrupts the global flow of fuel. The national average price for a gallon of gas was $4.47 on Sunday, up from $4.09 a month ago, according to the AAA motor club.

Trump has repeatedly pledged to end what he falsely calls an EV “mandate,” referring incorrectly to President Joe Biden’s target that half of all new vehicle sales be electric by 2030. No federal policy has mandated auto companies to sell EVs.

According to data from the automotive research group Edmunds, EVs accounted for 6.5% of new vehicle sales in February, down from 7.4% for all of 2025.

News of the revised standards immediately drew rebukes from environmentalists.

Dan Becker, director of the Center for Biological Diversity’s Safe Climate Transport Campaign, said that the final rule “ignores the feasibility of clean technology and the millions of fuel-efficient cars already on the road.”

“Trump is tanking sensible mile per gallon standards at the worst possible time for consumers, who are getting hit with sky-high prices at the pump,” Becker said in a statement. “Consumers will pay the price for these reckless rollbacks while Trump’s Big Oil and Big Auto buddies reap the short-term profits.”

Katherine García, director of the Sierra Club’s Clean Transportation for All campaign, vowed the environmental group would fight the rule and said that the loosening of fuel standards would “make driving more expensive too.”

“Less fuel-efficient cars mean more gas burned, spending more at the pump, and dirtier air in our communities,” Garcia wrote in a statement.

When the 2024 standards went into effect, NHTSA estimated they would save 14 billion gallons of gasoline from being burned by 2050. The agency also said that while new fuel-efficient vehicles cost more up front, savings on gasoline over the lifetime of the car or truck would more than make up for that.

Without these standards, in 2035, cars could produce 22,111 more tons of carbon dioxide per year than under the Biden-era rules. It also translates to an extra 90 tons a year of deadly soot particles and 4,870 additional tons a year of smog components such as nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds emitted into the air in coming years.

Mileage standards, known as the corporate average fuel economy, or CAFE, have been implemented since the 1970s energy crisis, and over time, automakers have gradually improved their vehicles’ average efficiency.

text:
Currently, only two nations in the world – the US and China – have fully commercialised robotaxis actively running on public roads.

Industry data from BloombergNEF indicates that the global operational fleet of roughly 10,000 autonomous vehicles (AVs) is expected to expand to 16,000 by the end of this year.

From a sustainability perspective, the rapid growth of autonomous mobility represents a critical pathway toward zero-emission urban transport.

As Frank Reig, CEO of EV fleet charging infrastructure provider Voltera, highlighted at Climate Week NYC, expanding autonomous fleets directly accelerates urban electrification: "Due to a lot of safety and technology reasons, AV equals EV.

"If you're commercialising an AV fleet in a certain market, you're now bringing forward electric mobility in that city. You're taking tailpipe out of that city."

Despite rapid commercial adoption across key hubs in the American South and California, deployment across the US remains starkly divided, creating a sharp contrast between progressive autonomous markets and cities like New York where human-driven internal combustion traffic continues to dominate.

Sustainable urban planning

While public attention frequently focuses on self-driving software, the core bottleneck for scaling zero-emission autonomous transport lies in the physical and spatial infrastructure required to service these fleets.

Frank explained that establishing dedicated fleet hubs in dense metropolitan areas represents the key operational hurdle: "Commercialising autonomous ride hail is really the long pole in the tent here is having the infrastructure in a city for charging, cleaning, servicing and data offload."

Voltera has developed infrastructure for over five years, operating more than 20 sites across key markets.

A standard charging site covers half an acre to one acre near high rideshare demand, featuring 40 to 60 fast-charging stalls, security booths, administrative facilities and dedicated IT infrastructure.

However, constructing these clean energy hubs requires overcoming three major physical and regulatory barriers:

Zoning and land use: Municipal land-use laws disqualify roughly 95% of available urban land, as commercial fleet depots are legally prohibited in most metropolitan areas.

Grid power allocation: Supplying 40 to 60 fast chargers requires securing 8 to 10 MW of electrical capacity – equivalent to the power demand of a major skyscraper – which local distribution grids struggle to deliver in high-density areas.

Permitting bureaucratic delays: Navigating local approvals adds prolonged friction, with Voltera often requiring over 100 distinct permits before a facility can become operational.

Addressing these land and grid challenges is essential for sustainable city design.

Frank argued that proactive planning allows municipalities to reclaim urban space from traditional car infrastructure: "Imagine if you could take out parking lots from city centres and maybe reuse some of the curved space more efficiently instead of just having it for car storage"

Beyond land efficiency, replacing human drivers with autonomous technology could substantially reduce the 1.1 million traffic fatalities occurring globally each year. Achieving a socially sustainable transition will, however, require upskilling professional drivers and supporting their transition into new employment sectors.

Grid resilience and flexible load integration

Integrating large fleets of high-utilisation electric vehicles into urban centres presents major strategic opportunities for energy management and grid decarbonisation.

In New York State, heating and powering buildings accounts for 40% of final energy consumption, making grid efficiency and emissions reduction a central environmental priority.

Doreen Harris, President and CEO of the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA), highlighted the broader climate impact of urban energy demands: "It is 40% of final energy use in New York State

Doreen noted the unique grid integration benefits offered by autonomous vehicles: "Autonomous vehicles are a huge opportunity for fast charging and a huge opportunity from a grid flexibility perspective as well."

As clean power generation grows, smart charging protocols and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) applications will enable AV depots to act as dynamic energy storage nodes.

Doreen said: "Flexibility is a very good thing in a highly decarbonised economy and frankly a highly decarbonised grid."

Municipal governance and sustainable transit integration

Alongside energy management, municipalities are working to integrate autonomous vehicles into broader local transport networks, emergency management frameworks and public transit systems.

In California, regulatory authority over autonomous vehicles rests with state bodies like the California Public Utilities Commission and the DMV, rather than local city governments.

Randall Winston, Deputy Mayor of Infrastructure and Climate Resilience for the City of Los Angeles, noted that LA has worked to bridge this gap by establishing an autonomous working group in late 2023.

To manage curb allocation and municipal assets sustainably, Los Angeles initiated digital infrastructure mapping programmes. As Randall said: "We were digitising our curve."

text:
Levi Strauss and Co. and Marks & Spencer (M&S) have launched the Fashion Renewable Collaborative (FRC), supported by Schneider Electric’s SE Advisory Services, to help fashion suppliers access renewable electricity and accelerate emissions reductions across global supply chains.

Fashion Brands Target Supply Chain Emissions

Levi Strauss and Co. and Marks & Spencer (M&S) have joined forces to launch an industry-wide programme designed to increase the adoption of renewable electricity across fashion supply chains.

The Fashion Renewable Collaborative (FRC) will provide participating suppliers with education, market guidance and support to assess and procure renewable electricity.

The initiative is supported by SE Advisory Services, Schneider Electric’s global consulting practice, which will act as the FRC’s global implementation partner.

The companies said textile processing, including fabric mills and dye houses, accounts for more than half of the apparel industry’s emissions, citing the Apparel Impact Institute.

According to the Roadmap to Net Zero from the World Resources Institute and Apparel Impact Institute, shifting manufacturing to renewable electricity represents around two-thirds of the sector’s identified emissions-reduction potential.

Suppliers Gain Renewable Electricity Support

The FRC has been established to address barriers preventing suppliers from adopting renewable electricity, including limited resources, fragmented engagement from brands and differing requirements from multiple customers.

Participating suppliers will have access to digital education through Resource Advisor+, SE Advisory Services’ artificial intelligence (AI)-native energy and sustainability intelligence platform.

Support will also cover renewable electricity options including power purchase agreements (PPAs), energy attribute certificates (EACs), on-site and distributed renewable generation and energy storage.

Katharine Beacham, Head of Sustainability and Materials in Fashion, Home and Beauty at M&S, said: “At M&S, we know that real change happens when we collaborate. Through our sustainability programme, Plan A, we’re committed to becoming a net zero business across our value chain by 2040, and that means working with others to make the transition to renewable electricity easier for our supply partners.

“Building on the work already underway through Re:Spark, our supply chain decarbonisation programme, the Fashion Renewable Collaborative will provide practical support, resources and greater access to renewable electricity, helping suppliers take action and facilitating change in the fashion supply chain.”

Collaborative Approach Aims to Reduce Supplier Burden

The FRC is designed to provide a common approach to renewable electricity engagement across participating fashion brands, reducing duplication for suppliers working with multiple customers.

Levi Strauss and M&S said their existing supplier engagement programmes have together registered nearly 500 supplier facilities.

“It’s become abundantly clear that the most effective way forward on emissions reduction is working in partnership with suppliers,” said Jennifer DuBuisson, Senior Director, Sustainability at Levi Strauss and Co.

“Initiatives like this create better working relationships and a more effective path forward. The Fashion Renewable Collaborative enables greater support of suppliers that want to access or would like to increase use of renewable electricity but haven’t been able to so far, helping facilitate adoption while reducing unnecessary duplication. It’s a natural extension of work we’ve already been doing with our own suppliers, and we’re glad to bring that experience into this effort with M&S and SE Advisory Services.”

Schneider Electric Supports Global Rollout

SE Advisory Services currently supports more than 20 supply chain decarbonisation initiatives globally, involving over 3,100 supplier companies and 16 multi-buyer renewable energy cohorts.

The FRC will use its Resource Advisor+ for Supply Chain product for supplier onboarding, readiness assessments, engagement tracking and progress monitoring.

“Many fashion brands have made their individual commitments. Now the focus must be on helping suppliers deliver against them,” said Steve Wilhite, Executive Vice President, SE Advisory Services.

“The Fashion Renewable Collaborative is designed to provide suppliers with practical support and engagement that can help accelerate renewable electricity adoption at scale. We’re excited to support Levi Strauss & Co. and M&S, and future participating brands as they work together to drive meaningful supply chain decarbonization.”

The FRC is now inviting more fashion brands to participate as sponsors and members, with the aim of expanding access to renewable electricity support and helping brands progress their individual supply chain decarbonisation targets.

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy said Sept. 24 it will help the Tennessee Valley Authority fund a $159.7 million effort to upgrade power lines in the South.

The announcement comes amid rapid data center growth and a federal push for U.S. AI dominance, increasing pressure for utility and transmission upgrades nationwide.

TVA, the nation’s largest public power provider, will share the cost of the upgrades, according to a press release from the energy department.

The seven-state utility requested $79.8 million from the energy department in its funding application. The project will help TVA increase the amount of electricity it can move across its transmission system by upgrading existing power lines and related technology.

The utility, TVA spokesperson Melissa Greene said, will put the money toward one transmission project that stretches across the Tennessee Valley region, along with five East Tennessee transmission line projects and one in Alabama.

In its application, TVA named the project "Rebuilding the Transmission Backbone for Energy and AI Dominance," echoing language that often emanates from a Trump administration stressing the value of American energy dominance.

TVA's project is one of 31 grid upgrades selected for federal funding. The energy department will provide $1.9 billion for the projects, while recipients are expected to contribute another $3.35 billion.

The projects aim to revamp or rebuild more than 1,500 miles of transmission lines and use new grid technologies to get real-time reads of line capacity, send additional power to lines with capacity to handle it and add new analytical tools to help operators react to changing conditions on the grid.

The projects should free up over 23 gigawatts of electricity capacity, according to the energy department, which has estimated the U.S. will need to expand its transmission systems by 60% by 2030.

TVA owns 16,400 miles of transmission lines and more than 100,000 transmission structures. The utility has 41 transmission system projects underway, as of Sept. 24.

Building new lines is often a lengthy process. A Congressional Research Service analyst in a 2022 report said it can take about a decade on average for permitting, financing and finishing new lines. A 2024 study from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory said clean energy projects often spent about five years in the approval process amid studies on transmission tech.

TVA is a federal organization and is funded by ratepayers, who ultimately provide the bulk of the money for the utility's share of the project cost. The utility does not receive appropriations from Congress.

description:
NEW YORK (AP) — The Trump administration on Monday plans to release new fuel economy standards that would relax regulatory requirements for automakers to control pollution from gasoline-powered cars and light trucks.

The change would further Trump’s promise to revoke policies that encouraged or created incentives for the production of electric vehicles.
Without these standards, in 2035, cars could produce 22,111 more tons of carbon dioxide per year than under the Biden-era rules.
